name: The Intermediate Value Theorem
statement: A continuous function that takes two values also takes every value in between.
statementAccent: also takes every value in between
meaning: The intermediate value theorem states that if a continuous function on a closed interval takes one value at the left endpoint and another at the right, then it takes every value between those two somewhere inside the interval. A continuous curve cannot jump from below a level to above it without crossing that level. The most-used special case, Bolzano's theorem, says that a continuous function which is negative at one end and positive at the other must be zero somewhere in between, guaranteeing a root. It is one of the first deep consequences of continuity, capturing the intuitive idea that an unbroken curve cannot skip values, and it depends on the completeness of the real number line.
mechanism: The theorem is a direct expression of what continuity and the completeness of the reals mean together. Continuity forbids the function from jumping, so its graph is an unbroken curve; completeness guarantees that the real line has no gaps for a target value to slip through. Formally, to reach a value between the endpoint values, one considers the set of points where the function stays below the target and takes its least upper bound, which completeness guarantees exists; continuity then forces the function to equal the target exactly there. The result holds for any continuous real-valued function on a connected interval and is the one-dimensional face of the deeper topological fact that continuous images of connected sets are connected.

examples.text: If a continuous function is negative at one point and positive at another, it must equal zero somewhere between them, the basis of the bisection method for finding roots.
A square table on an uneven floor can always be rotated to a position where all four legs touch, a playful consequence proved using the intermediate value theorem.
On any great circle of the earth there are two opposite points with the same temperature, a one-dimensional case of the Borsuk-Ulam theorem provable from this result.

variants.name: Bolzano's theorem
variants.text: The special case of a sign change: a continuous function negative at one end and positive at the other has a root between them, the form most used in practice.

variants.name: The topological form
variants.text: The generalisation that a continuous function maps connected sets to connected sets, of which the interval version is the one-dimensional instance.

whyItMatters: The intermediate value theorem is a foundational result of real analysis and a first payoff of making continuity precise, and it does practical work by guaranteeing solutions to equations without solving them. It justifies numerical root-finding methods like bisection, supplies existence proofs across mathematics, from fixed-point theorems to the fundamental theorem of algebra, and models countless real situations where a quantity passing between two values must pass through everything in between.

working.text: find points where a continuous function has opposite signs; the theorem then guarantees a zero between them, even with no formula for it.
use the sign-change guarantee to trap a root in an interval and repeatedly halve it, the bisection method built on the theorem.
remember the result needs both an unbroken function and a gapless real line, so it fails for discontinuous functions or over the rationals.

limits: The theorem requires the function to be continuous on the whole interval; a single jump discontinuity can let it skip values, so continuity is essential. It also depends on the completeness of the real numbers and fails over the rationals, where a continuous function can change sign without ever hitting zero, since the crossing point may be irrational. And it is purely an existence statement: it guarantees that some point achieves the intermediate value but says nothing about where it is, how many such points there are, or how to compute one, only that at least one exists.
misreadings: The theorem guarantees a value is attained but does not locate it or count how often, so it is existence without construction. It needs genuine continuity: for a function with a jump, the conclusion can fail, so it is not enough for the function merely to be defined at every point. And it is specific to the real numbers' completeness; over the rationals a continuous function can pass from negative to positive without ever equalling zero, because the root it would need is irrational and simply missing from the rationals.
origin: Proved rigorously by Bernard Bolzano in 1817 in his paper on the sign-change form, part of the nineteenth-century effort to give calculus firm foundations, with related ideas in Cauchy's contemporaneous work on continuity.
